title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (1 of 7)
hook: a new camp opens with a text so short it fits on one page
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Gita. Eighteen chapters, and your line was: you actually read it. Today the path goes underneath it. Day two hundred thirty-two.

Camp five is called the depths. We start by going underneath the Gita, to the older texts it draws on. They're called the Upanishads, and the Gita quotes them, borrows their pictures, sometimes their exact verses. Many texts carry the name, and tradition sets apart a small group as the principal ones. We'll spend a week each on four of them. And we start with one of the shortest. Eighteen verses. It fits on one page, and people have written whole books about its first line.
screen: `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS.` → `UNDERNEATH THE GITA.` → `EIGHTEEN VERSES.`

segments.voice: The word Upanishad is usually explained as sitting down near: upa, near, ni, down, shad, to sit. A student sitting close to a teacher, close enough to hear something said quietly. That's the feel of these texts. Not a law code, not a hymnbook. A conversation near the fire. The Isha Upanishad is named after its first word. Isha means the Lord, the one who rules. The verse opens: isha vasyam idam sarvam. All this, whatever moves in this moving world, is vasyam by the Lord. And that one word, vasyam, can be read two ways. Some commentators read it as dwelt in, pervaded: the Lord lives inside everything, the way salt lives in seawater. The great teacher Shankara read it as covered, clothed: wrap everything you see in the thought of the Lord, the way you'd wrap a gift. Either way, the claim is enormous. Not some things. All this. The coffee cup. The traffic. The person you find difficult. The verse doesn't stop there; the second half is where our week's word comes from, and it's tomorrow's lesson. But hold the first half for a day, because everything else in the Upanishad leans on it. If all this belongs to the Lord, then nothing here is only mine. And it also means nothing here is only ordinary. Mahatma Gandhi is often quoted as saying that if all the other scriptures were lost and only this first verse remained, Hinduism would live on. That's a lot of weight for one line. This week we'll see if it can carry it.
screen: `UPANISHAD: SITTING DOWN NEAR.` · `ISHA: THE LORD.` · `DWELT IN, OR CLOTHED.` · `NOT SOME THINGS. ALL THIS.` · then, large: `ALL THIS IS PERVADED BY THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, and let your eyes rest on whatever is in front of you. A wall, a window, your own hands. Don't analyze it. Just try the verse on it: all this. Whatever your tradition calls the sacred, or simply life itself, imagine it living inside the thing you're looking at. Then close your eyes and try it on the sounds around you. Then on your own breath. If you pray, you can say the two words isha vasyam quietly. If not, just notice. The bell holds the time.
Renounce and enjoy. The whole teaching of the Isha's first verse. Today we took the first half: all this is pervaded by the Lord. Tomorrow, the renouncing and the enjoying.
Your line: renounce, and enjoy. For today, just the ground under it. Pick one ordinary thing, your cup, your street, and once, look at it as if it were lived in. Day two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Hindus know the Isha Upanishad's first verse by heart, and it is often chanted along with the 'purnam adah' peace invocation that traditionally opens the text.

trapdoor: what you thought: an upanishad is a secret scripture.
what it means: the word pictures sitting down near a teacher, close enough to hear.
what a scholar hears: upa-ni-shad, near-down-sit; the Isha is also the fortieth chapter of the Vajasaneyi Samhita of the White Yajurveda.
